title: Onam 2026: How Chefs Are Reimagining the Traditional Kerala Feast
excerpt: From erissery hummus to bone marrow ularthiyathu, India's top chefs are rethinking the Onasadya while luxury hotels keep the classic banana-leaf spread alive for a new generation.
body:
• Onam 2026 celebrations are underway across India, with Thiruvonam — the main feast day — bringing the traditional Onasadya to millions of tables
  • Chefs like Hussain Shahzad and Manu Chandra are reimagining the sadya with dishes like erissery hummus, scallop carpaccio, and Malabar dry-aged duck roast that reflect Kerala's multicultural history
  • Luxury hotels from Gurugram to Mumbai are offering traditional banana-leaf spreads curated by Kerala-born master chefs, keeping authenticity alive outside the state
  • The modern Onasadya movement challenges the perception that the feast is purely vegetarian, drawing on Kerala's diverse communities including Nasrani Christians and Mappila Muslims

A Feast That Tells a Story

The Onasadya — the elaborate banana-leaf feast at the heart of Onam celebrations — has been served in Kerala homes for centuries. Typically 15 to 20 dishes laid out in a precise arrangement, it is a vegetarian spread tied to the harvest festival and the mythical return of King Mahabali. But in 2026, a growing number of chefs are asking a different question: what if the sadya could tell a broader story about Kerala itself?

At restaurants across Mumbai, Delhi, and Bengaluru, chefs are creating Onam-inspired menus that push beyond the traditional format while respecting its roots. The approach is less about replacing the classic sadya and more about expanding what the feast can represent.

Reimagining the Banana Leaf

Chefs Hussain Shahzad and Manu Chandra have built their reimagined Onam experience around Kerala's cultural diversity. Their menu includes a "Thali of Unity" featuring dishes from the state's different communities — Malayali Hindu, Nasrani Christian, and Mappila Muslim traditions — served alongside creative reinterpretations of classic preparations.

Among the standout dishes: erissery hummus, inspired by the Arab traders who used Kerala's ports for the spice trade. Traditionally, pumpkin erissery is a mandatory sadya item. The chefs transformed it into a chip-and-dip format that references Kerala's historical connections to the Middle East while making the dish more approachable for grazing-style dining.

"Until the 19th century, several marginalised Hindu groups as well as Muslims and Christians did include meat dishes in their Onam fare. The standardised, homogenised Onam sadya is a relatively recent creation."

— Manu S. Pillai, Historian

Their menu also includes bone marrow and short rib ularthiyathu, broccoli olan gratin, scallop carpaccio, Malabar dry-aged duck roast, and sulaimani cheesecake — dishes that would be unrecognizable on a traditional banana leaf but draw directly from Kerala's culinary traditions.

The Traditional Sadya Holds Strong

While experimental menus draw attention, the traditional Onasadya remains the centerpiece of celebrations. Across India, luxury hotels are offering elaborate banana-leaf feasts curated by Kerala-born chefs, ensuring authenticity for the diaspora community celebrating far from home.

At The Leela Ambience Gurugram, MasterChef Asai Thambi has curated a classic vegetarian Sadhya available from August 16 to 25. The spread includes matta rice, avial, sambar, olan, beans thoran, vellarikka pachadi, thakkali rasam, kai upperi, puli inji, crisp papadum, and the essential ada pradhaman and parippu payasam — each dish occupying its designated position on the banana leaf.

ITC Master Chef Creations is offering a ready-to-enjoy Sadhya meal delivered through Swiggy and Zomato, featuring red pumpkin erissery, cabbage thoran, parippu with ghee, sharkara upperi, and ada pradhaman — bringing the home-cooked festival experience to families who may lack the time or ingredients for the full preparation.

More Than a Vegetarian Meal

Historian Manu S. Pillai has been instrumental in contextualizing the Onasadya within Kerala's complex social history. He points out that Onam is not exclusively a Hindu festival — it is a comprehensive Malayali celebration observed across communities. The idea that the sadya must be strictly vegetarian is, historically speaking, a relatively recent standardization.

This perspective has given chefs the cultural license to include meat and seafood preparations in their Onam menus without feeling they are betraying tradition. Rather, they argue they are recovering an older, more inclusive version of it.

What's Next

For the Indian diaspora in the United States, Onam celebrations have become an important marker of cultural identity. Malayali associations across the country organize community sadyas, Pookalam (floral rangoli) competitions, and Thiruvathira dance performances. The trend of reimagined Onam feasts is beginning to reach diaspora communities too, with pop-up dinners and chef collaborations bringing modern Kerala cuisine to cities like New York, San Francisco, and Houston.

Whether served on a banana leaf in a Kerala courtyard or reimagined in a Mumbai restaurant, the Onasadya remains what it has always been at its core: a celebration of abundance, togetherness, and the harvest that sustains a culture.
nri_angle: Malayali associations across the U.S. organize community sadyas during Onam, and the reimagined feast trend is reaching diaspora communities through pop-up dinners and chef collaborations.
